why.dayLabour.title: Day labour pays about

why.handSkill.lesson: A hand who stays gets better.

why.hut.title: A hand's hut

why.free.title: Labourers free today

why.away.Sick: On a sick day you rest.

why.report.household: Living costs come before anything else.
why.report.finance: A loan helps only if what it buys earns more than this.

why.report.netResult: This is your profit for the season.

letter.welcome: My dear beta, the farm is yours now. Six acres by the river, the hut your grandfather built, and the well that never failed us. The fields have rested too long and the soil is tired, but it is honest: it gives back what you put in. You'll find seed potato, some wheat and lentils, and greens seed in the store, and a little money to begin. Start small.
letter.garden: By the door is the baadi, our kitchen garden. Radish, spinach, coriander: they grow in minutes and feed the house. Sow one bed now; by the time you've looked around, it will be ready.
letter.household: A farm runs on the people who work it, and you are the first. Choose how the house eats and how long you work: good food and rest let you do more, day after day. The house eats from the store first. Your grandfather kept wheat and lentils from his last harvest; if you'd rather sow them than eat them, switch 'eat from the store' off for now.
letter.firstPick: There: your first basket. Everything you pick goes to the store, where it waits for you. Greens don't keep long, so eat them or sell them soon.
letter.firstSale: The trader comes to the gate every day and buys at a fair, low price. That's money today. His truck comes every morning at 6:00 and leaves at midnight. Later you'll learn when it pays to wait, or to take a cart to the mandi in town.
letter.longCrop: Now something that takes longer. Potato does well in Spring on the well acres, and the seed is already in the store. It takes about 15 hours. Crops wait in the field when they're ready, but not forever: after three days they start to spoil.
letter.comeBack: That's a good first day. The farm keeps going while you're away: the crops grow, the house eats, the trader buys. Your {crop} will be ready {time}.{quick} Want a nudge when it's ready? Never at night.
letter.comeBack.on: That's a good first day. The farm keeps going while you're away: the crops grow, the house eats, the trader buys. Your {crop} will be ready {time}.{quick}
letter.comeBack.quick: Your other acres needn't wait: sown now, {crops}.
letter.firstReturn: Welcome back. Here's what happened while you were away. Tap Collect all to bring in what's ready.
letter.firstFieldHarvest: Your first field harvest. Tap the ? beside it to see what made it: the soil, the water, your care, the weather, the seed. The weakest of them holds the rest back.
letter.pest: Pests on one of your fields. Spray now and you'll save most of the crop; leave it and you'll lose some. Fields that grow the same crop again and again draw more pests.
letter.sellOrStore: Your store is filling up. Three ways to sell: the trader at the gate (today, at his price), the village market (a little at a time, at a better price), or a cart to the mandi (a full load, half a day away, after the cart's hire). Or keep it for a better season, if it keeps.
letter.seasonReport: Your first season is done. The report shows whether the farm paid for itself. Money you paid ahead for next season isn't a cost yet, so cash and profit tell different stories.
letter.labour: Your fields need more hands than yours. A labourer from the next village stays for one crop, till its harvest; a farm hand stays for the season but needs a hut to live in. A Hamlet begins with a hand's house.
letter.borrowing: Money is short for what you want to do next. The moneylender lends quickly, at a high price. The bank lends more, cheaper, if you can show land or a good season. Borrow only what the work will pay back.
letter.sick: You're unwell today and the fields will wait. Eat well, rest, and the chemist in the village has medicine.
letter.hamlet: Look at what you've built: six acres in good heart, a house for a hand, a season that paid its way. This isn't a homestead any more. It's a Hamlet, and you can keep cattle now: tap your cattle yard beside the house. A Village needs more: five households on your land, a business that pays its way two seasons, and a school for the children. Your letter in the Menu keeps count.
letter.village: Beta, your grandfather used to say a village isn't its fields, it's its people. Look around: five families make their homes on your land, your {business} has paid its way, and the children walk to the school you gave them. It's a Village now. New trades open to you: a bakery and a dairy, stalls on the square, drip and a borewell for the fields, a tractor, and the co-op bank will lend you more. Grow it with care: every family here counts on you.
letter.firstOrders: A shop in the city buys fresh produce straight from farms. It pays more than the trader, but only for what you harvest today, delivered by midnight, and it pays the next morning.
letter.truckAway: The trader's truck comes at 6:00 and leaves at midnight, or when it's full. The stall closes at night too. Keep it in the store, or take a cart to the mandi.

why.era.title: Becoming a Hamlet
why.era.acres: Field harvests on different acres you own count, all in the same season. A second harvest on the same acre doesn't add an acre. A new season starts the count again.
why.era.care: The average Care of every field harvest this season, as a share of what the crops needed. More hands than the crops need lift it a little; too few hold it back.
why.era.hut: A hand's hut in the labour quarters, finished. One being built doesn't count yet.
why.era.profit: Any closed season whose farm profit was above nothing: the farm earned more than its seed, inputs, wages and upkeep cost.
why.village.title: Becoming a Village
why.village.households: A household is a family in a house on your land, or a hand alone in his hut. Build a family house and a family moves in: the co-op bank lends on the house, and the rent pays the loan back.
why.village.business: A season counts when the business's own books show a profit after its costs and wages, in any two seasons. Start a flour mill; its Books show each season.
why.village.school: Build the school on the school plot, from cash or with a co-op loan.
why.village.lesson: Quickest: homes first, then a business, then the school. The bank lends on a house and its rent repays it; borrow for a business first and the bank has less left for houses.
why.era.lesson: Six acres is more than one founder can tend: the Hamlet starts when you hire.

why.plan.rent: The council's rent for a pitch in the square, {rent} a season, paid upfront. A shop on your own acre pays none.
why.books.sales.shop: What customers paid at the counter.
why.books.goods.shop: What the goods sold cost the shop, and stock thrown away unsold. Your own produce and products come in at the trader's price.
why.books.margin.shop: Sales less the cost of what was sold. It has to pay the running costs.
why.books.cashIn.shop: Sales and any cash you put in.
why.books.cashOut.shop: Stock, wages, rent, repairs and any cash you took out.
why.books.stock.shop: What's on the counter and in the back, at what it cost.
why.books.rent: The council's rent for the pitch, paid upfront each season.
books.why.noOwn.shop: It sold nothing: nothing put out, nobody to run it, or no cash for stock
why.businessCash.own.shop: The shop's own money, apart from yours: what you put in and its sales in; stock, rent and wages out.
why.businessHours.area.shop: Customers come between 8:00 and 20:00; open fewer hours and those hours' customers go to the other shops.
why.businessHours.you.shop: You're at the shop these hours, so they come off your farm work.
why.businessMarket.price.veg_stall: What your store can't give, the stall buys at the local market each morning, as a sabziwala does at the mandi: vegetables and fruit at the market's price. Pav, paneer and curd your bakery and dairy can't give come at the import price.
why.businessMarket.lesson.veg_stall: Bought in, a good earns only the markup: your own produce, at the trader's price, earns the most.
why.businessMarket.price.tea_stall: After your herd's milk, the tea stall buys neighbours' milk at 6:00 up to its milk a day, at the co-op's price and a little more; and its snacks at the market when your bakery has none.
why.businessMarket.lesson.tea_stall: Stop buying and it works only your herd's milk: fewer cups when you run short.
why.businessMarket.price.sweet_shop: What your dairy and mill can't give, it buys at the market's import price.
why.businessMarket.lesson.sweet_shop: Your own paneer, ghee and atta make the margin: market ones cost more.
why.businessOverdraft.draws.shop: When its cash can't pay for stock, rent, repairs, a wage or a loan payment, the bank pays and the overdraft grows; money coming in pays it off first.
why.businessOverdraft.past.shop: Past the limit it can't buy stock, so its counter empties; at the close a wage it can't pay goes unpaid: the worker leaves.
why.businessClose.stock.shop: What's left in stock is sold to the trader at today's price.
why.recipeMade.recipe.rasgulla.sweet_sho: Half a kilo of paneer, kneaded and boiled in syrup, makes a kilo of rasgulla: {batch} a batch.
why.recipeMade.recipe.atta_laddoo.sweet_: Atta roasted in ghee with sugar, rolled by hand: {batch} a batch.

why.shopShare.how: Each hour, people share themselves between the shops open by their pull: a shop's share is its pull over all the shops' pulls. A shop that runs out passes the rest on.
why.shopShare.lesson: Customers weigh more than price: a shop nearby, with no queue and a good name, wins them too.
why.shopShare.rival.grocer: The village's own grocer, on the main street: the usual price, never runs out, never closes.
why.shopShare.rival.village_tea: The village's own tea stall: the usual price, open from 6:00 to 22:00; it serves 200 cups an hour at most.
why.shopShare.rival.town_halwai: The halwai in the town, 1,500 m past the square: good sweets, but a long walk.
why.shopToday.title: {name}: served today
why.shopToday.hours: People come between {open} and {close}, a little each hour.
why.shopToday.short: Some who chose it went elsewhere: it ran out or was full.
why.shopToday.all: It served everyone who chose it.
why.shopToday.lesson: A customer turned away is a sale for someone else.
why.shopLost.title: Customers no shop served today
why.shopLost.how: When every shop of the kind is closed, full or out of stock, people go without: they make tea at home or buy at the weekly market.
why.shopLost.lesson: A gap no shop fills is a chance for a shop.
why.shopPeople.title: People who shop

why.shopDemand.each.veg: A person's vegetables and fruit a day
why.shopDemand.adults: Of them, those who drink chai

why.shopDemand.how.veg: Shared between the vegetables, potatoes most, coriander least; your pav, paneer and curd as the village shops buy them.
why.shopDemand.how.chai: A real day is about 23 days of life: a few cups a day add up.
why.shopDemand.how.sweets: Shared evenly between rasgulla and laddoo.

why.shopReference.veg: The local market's price for each, + {pct}: what a stall charges in the village. Your products: the trader's price + {pct}.
why.shopReference.chai: What a cup costs in the village.
why.shopReference.sweets: What a kilo costs at the town's halwai.
why.shopReference.lesson: Customers compare your price with this: cheaper wins them, dearer loses some.
why.shopPrice.title: Your price
why.shopPrice.fewer: Dearer, and some go elsewhere, and fewer buy at all.
why.shopPrice.lesson: Underpricing wins customers but loses margin.
why.shopExpected.title: Your share on a pitch
why.shopExpected.yours: Your pull: the usual price, standard, 2.5 stars, no queue
why.shopExpected.how: Your share is your pull over all the shops' pulls: the village's customers, from the square.
why.pitchRent.title: Pitch rent a season
why.pitchRent.how: Paid to the council upfront: when you open, then at each close for the season ahead.
why.pitchRent.lesson: A pitch costs rent, but the whole village passes by.
why.shopPutOut.title: {good} a day
why.shopPutOut.store: Taken from your store at 6:00, at the trader's price: your farm sells it, the stall pays. What your store can't give is bought at the local market's price, if you allow it.
why.shopPutOut.yours: From your bakery or dairy at 6:00, at the trader's price, before the village shops buy; else the market's, if you allow it.
why.shopMilk.title: Milk in stock
why.shopMilk.how: At the 6:00 milking the tea stall takes your herd's milk first, at the co-op's price, before your dairy; then neighbours', if you allow it. Yesterday's milk spoils. A stall that opens later in the day buys neighbours' milk that hour.
why.shopStars.title: {name}'s stars
why.shopStars.served: Served {pct} of those who chose it
why.shopStars.how: Each night the stars move a tenth of the way to the day's score. Serving everyone who comes is worth 2 points, standard quality 1 point and good quality 1.5 points, value up to 1 point (none at 30% above the usual price); 4.5 points make 5 stars. One day shut is forgiven; from the second in a row, a shut day scores as if nobody was served.
why.shopStars.lesson: Reputation is earned slowly and lost fast: running out, or a long queue, costs more than a cheap price earns.
why.shopQuality.title: Quality
why.shopQuality.veg: Good quality puts out only fresh produce: whatever is left at night is cleared at 6:00 as spoilage, then the day's goods go out. Standard quality keeps leftovers, spoiling at their rate.
why.shopQuality.chai: Good chai is made with full-cream milk: more milk a cup, the dearest part of a cup. The milk a day goes up with it, for the same cups. At the usual price it costs more than it brings, and a price above the usual can bring a newcomer to set up against you (an even chance each season). Good chai wins customers and stars; standard chai makes the money.
why.shopQuality.sweets: Good sweets use pure ghee and fresh paneer, and nothing is kept overnight: what's left at night is cleared at 6:00 as spoilage.
why.shopQuality.cupMilk: Milk a good cup ({standard} at standard)
why.shopQuality.lesson: Quality costs every day and pays slowly, in customers and in stars.

why.school.gift: A gift to the village: once built it's the district's school, not yours. Your net worth falls by its cost; your farm's profit doesn't, so the bank's room isn't cut.
why.school.teacher: The district posts the teacher and pays the wage, as in any government primary school.
why.school.lesson: Public goods pay back to the town, not to the one who pays: in your people's reading, and in what they earn.
why.schoolUpkeep.title: The school's upkeep
why.schoolUpkeep.text: Paid at each season's close, a gift to the village. Short of cash, it goes unpaid that season and the district carries the school.

codex.diminishingReturns.title: Diminishing returns
codex.diminishingReturns.text: Each extra unit of an input adds less than the one before, and past a point it adds nothing. A field already near its best gains little from more fertiliser.
codex.diminishingReturns.numbers: On a field you gave chemical fertiliser, everything together came to {n0} the usual yield, but no field gives more than {n1}: the last of the fertiliser bought nothing.
codex.diminishingReturns.world: Farmers who doubled their urea over the decades got far less than double the wheat: the soil and the plant set a ceiling.
codex.soilFertility.title: Soil fertility
codex.soilFertility.text: Fertility is the soil's store of food for plants. Every crop draws on it; lentils, a fallow season and compost put it back. Run it down and every later crop yields less.
codex.soilFertility.numbers: A harvest left one of your acres at fertility {n0} of 100. That crop uses about {n1} a season; compost puts back more than a crop takes.
codex.soilFertility.world: Indian farmers rotate wheat or rice with pulses and spread farmyard manure to keep their soil from running down.
codex.opportunityCost.title: Opportunity cost
codex.opportunityCost.text: The opportunity cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it. An hour spent one way can't be spent another.
codex.opportunityCost.numbers: You earned {n0} at day labour while {n1} of your own acres stood empty.
codex.opportunityCost.world: A farmer who works for wages in town at sowing time earns cash now, but may lose a season's crop on his own land.
codex.profitNotCash.title: Profit is not cash
codex.profitNotCash.text: Profit is what a season earned less what it cost. Cash is the money in hand. Money can leave without being a cost (a loan repaid, a gift, seed bought ahead) and arrive without being income (a loan taken).
codex.profitNotCash.numbers: A season ended with a profit of {n0}, yet your cash changed by {n1}.
codex.profitNotCash.world: A shop can show a profit and still run out of money to pay its supplier. That's why businesses keep a profit and loss statement and a cash flow statement.
codex.interest.title: Interest and compounding
codex.interest.text: Interest is the price of borrowing: a share of what you owe, each season. Left unpaid, interest joins the debt and earns interest itself: that is compounding.
codex.interest.numbers: Last season your loans cost {n0} in interest, on {n1} still owed.
codex.interest.world: At 6% a season, a debt left unpaid doubles in about three years; at a bank's 2.5% a season, in about seven.
codex.creditScore.title: Credit score
codex.creditScore.text: A credit score sums up how you've handled debt: paying on time raises it, missing a payment lowers it. Lenders lend more, and cheaper, to a higher score.
codex.creditScore.numbers: Your credit score went from {n0} to {n1}.
codex.creditScore.world: In India, credit scores such as CIBIL's run from 300 to 900, and banks look at them before every loan.
codex.leverage.title: Leverage
codex.leverage.text: Leverage is using borrowed money to do more than your own money allows. It multiplies a good season's gain, and a bad season's loss.
codex.leverage.numbers: You borrowed {n0}, more than your last season's farm profit of {n1}.
codex.leverage.world: A tractor bought on a loan pays if it earns more than its instalments; in a drought year the instalments still come.
codex.liquidity.title: Liquidity
codex.liquidity.text: Liquidity is how quickly what you own can become cash. Land and buildings are worth a lot but take time to sell; a bill wants cash today.
codex.liquidity.numbers: You had {n0} in cash when a payment was refused, though you owned {n1} in land, buildings, stock and more.
codex.liquidity.world: Many farmers are land-rich and cash-poor: they borrow at sowing time though they own acres worth lakhs.
codex.inflation.title: Inflation
codex.inflation.text: Inflation is prices rising over time. The same coins buy less: seed, wages and land cost more, and what you sell fetches more too.
codex.inflation.numbers: Prices in the region are now {n0} above where your farm started.
codex.inflation.world: Prices in India have risen by around 5% a year on average: what cost 100 rupees in 2010 cost about 200 by 2024.
codex.workingCapital.title: Working capital
codex.workingCapital.text: Working capital is the money a business needs between paying for its inputs and wages and being paid for what it sells. With too little, it borrows to keep going.
codex.workingCapital.numbers: Your business is using {n0} of its overdraft, which goes up to {n1}.
codex.workingCapital.world: A kirana shop buys stock on credit from its wholesaler and pays once customers have bought it: that credit is its working capital.
codex.grossMargin.title: Gross margin
codex.grossMargin.text: Gross margin is what's left of sales after the cost of the goods sold, before wages, rent and other costs. It has to pay for everything else.
codex.grossMargin.numbers: Your business sold {n0} last season, and the goods it sold cost {n1}: a gross margin of {n2}.
codex.grossMargin.world: A halwai's milk and sugar cost about half a sweet's price; the other half pays the cook, the shop and his profit.
codex.fixedVariable.title: Fixed and variable costs
codex.fixedVariable.text: Variable costs rise and fall with what you sell, like ingredients. Fixed costs stay the same whatever you sell, like a wage or a rent. When sales fall, fixed costs don't.
codex.fixedVariable.numbers: Your business's sales fell from {n0} to {n1}, but its wage and rent still came to {n2}.
codex.fixedVariable.world: A tea stall pays its pitch rent in a slow week just as in a busy one; only the milk it buys goes down with the customers.
codex.breakEven.title: Break-even
codex.breakEven.text: A business breaks even when its sales just cover all its costs. Below that it loses money; above it, every extra sale adds profit.
codex.breakEven.numbers: Your business's plan expected {n0} of sales a season against {n1} of costs.
codex.breakEven.world: Before a bank lends to a new shop, it asks how many customers a day the shop needs to break even, and whether the street has them.
codex.forecastActual.title: Forecast and actual
codex.forecastActual.text: A forecast is your best guess before you start. Comparing it with what happened shows which guesses were wrong, so the next plan is better.
codex.forecastActual.numbers: Your business's plan expected a profit of {n0} a season; it has made {n1} a season on average.
codex.forecastActual.world: Companies compare their budget with their actual results every quarter; the gaps teach them more than the forecast did.
codex.unitEconomics.title: Unit economics
codex.unitEconomics.text: Unit economics is the profit or loss on one unit: what one kilo or one item costs to make against what it sells for. If one unit loses money, selling more loses more.
codex.unitEconomics.numbers: A kilo of what your business makes costs {n0} to make and sells for about {n1}.
codex.unitEconomics.world: A chaiwala knows to the paisa what a cup's milk, tea and sugar cost: that's what tells him his price.
codex.depreciation.title: Depreciation
codex.depreciation.text: Depreciation is the cost of an asset wearing out, spread over its useful life. No cash moves, but the asset is worth a little less each season.
codex.depreciation.numbers: Last season your buildings and machines wore down by {n0}; they're now on your books at {n1}.
codex.depreciation.world: A tractor bought for 6 lakh may be worth half that after seven or eight years of work.
codex.appreciation.title: Appreciation
codex.appreciation.text: Appreciation is an asset growing in value, like land as prices rise and the village grows. It only becomes money when you sell.
codex.appreciation.numbers: Land you paid {n0} for is now worth {n1}.
codex.appreciation.world: Farmland near growing towns in India has often risen in price faster than prices in general.
codex.yield.title: Yield
codex.yield.text: Yield is the income an asset pays each season or year, as a share of what it cost. It lets you compare a house, a deposit or a shop.
codex.yield.numbers: A family paid you {n0} in rent this season: {n1} of what their house cost you.
codex.yield.world: A house in an Indian city often yields 2–4% a year in rent, while a bank deposit pays 6–7%.
codex.hiringUncertainty.title: Hiring under uncertainty
codex.hiringUncertainty.text: When you hire, you can't see how good someone will be; you guess from what you can learn. A reference check costs a little and narrows the guess.
codex.hiringUncertainty.numbers: You paid {n0} to check an applicant's reference before deciding.
codex.hiringUncertainty.world: Employers call a candidate's last employer because a bad hire costs far more than the call.
codex.marketWage.title: The market wage
codex.marketWage.text: The market wage is what workers can earn elsewhere. Offer less and the good ones go to whoever pays it.
codex.marketWage.numbers: You offered {n0}; the applicant asked for {n1} instead.
codex.marketWage.world: When building work booms in a district, farm wages there rise too: labourers can earn more on the sites.
codex.retention.title: Retention
codex.retention.text: Retention is keeping the people you have. Replacing a skilled worker costs more than a fair raise: the search, the training and the work lost meanwhile.
codex.retention.numbers: Your worker is paid {n0} a season; another employer offered {n1}.
codex.retention.world: Businesses often find it cheaper to match an offer than to hire and train someone new.
codex.trainingRoi.title: Return on training
codex.trainingRoi.text: Return on investment compares what something cost with what it brings back. A course costs money and days away; a more skilled worker gives more for years.
codex.trainingRoi.numbers: A course raised your worker's skill to {n0}.
codex.trainingRoi.world: Governments pay for skills training because a trained worker earns and produces more for the rest of their working life.
codex.employerReputation.title: Employer reputation
codex.employerReputation.text: Your reputation as an employer is what workers hear about you: fair pay, paid on time, help when it's needed. Good workers come to a good name, and stay.
codex.employerReputation.numbers: Your name as an employer now stands at {n0}.
codex.employerReputation.world: In a village everyone knows who pays on time; a bad name empties the queue at your gate.
codex.publicGoods.title: Public goods
codex.publicGoods.text: A public good is one everyone can use, and one person's use doesn't take from another's: a school, a road, a clean pond. Nobody can sell it for a profit, so it's built when someone gives it or the government does.
codex.publicGoods.numbers: The school you gave cost {n0}. Children at it now, free: {n1}.
codex.publicGoods.world: Most of India's village schools, roads and wells were built by the government or by donors, not by markets.
codex.longTermInvestment.title: Long-term investment
codex.longTermInvestment.text: A long-term investment pays back slowly, over years, not seasons. A child who can read will earn more all their life.
codex.longTermInvestment.numbers: A child finished {n0} years at your school and can read; the school cost you {n1}.
codex.longTermInvestment.world: Studies across India find each extra year of schooling raises a person's earnings by around 5–10%.

stmt.people.none: Nobody worked for you this season.

stmt.people.rep.why: Workers hear how you treat people. Paying on time and fairly raises your name; a wage you couldn't pay or a raise refused lowers it. A good name makes hiring easier.
stmt.people.whyPaid: Paid for the season (house rent included)
stmt.people.whyAsked: Would ask today for their skill
stmt.people.outcome.why.0: They stayed on for the new season.
stmt.people.outcome.why.1: The new season's wage couldn't be paid, so the contract lapsed. They wait a few days, then leave unless you pay.
stmt.people.outcome.why.2: They took an offer elsewhere, or were refused a raise they asked for, and left at the close.
stmt.people.outcome.why.3: The new season's wage wasn't paid, so they left.
stmt.people.outcome.why.4: Their working years are done, so their contract wasn't renewed.
stmt.group.1: What you bought, sold or saved
stmt.cash.notKept: Kept from your next season on
stmt.cash.notKeptNote: This season closed before cash flow was itemised. Its start and end cash are above.
stmt.bs.note: Land and stored goods are at market value; buildings, animals and machines at book. A statement stays as it was counted then: it is a record.
stmt.bs.cash.why: The cash you had in hand when the books closed.
stmt.bs.deposit.why: Money kept in the co-operative bank's savings deposit. It earns interest and is never taken without your say.
stmt.bs.prepaid.why: Living costs, wages and rent paid now for the season ahead. Yours until the season uses them up.
stmt.bs.owed.why: What the supermarket owed you for deliveries, paid at 6:00.
stmt.bs.goods.why: Grain, fruit, seed and feed in your store, at today's market price.
stmt.bs.land.why: Every acre you own at today's price. A quick sale to a neighbour fetches 80% of it.
stmt.bs.buildings.why: What you paid for your buildings less the wear counted each season.
stmt.bs.trees.why: Trees you planted, at what they cost, less what they have given back.
stmt.bs.livestock.why: Your animals at what you paid. They don't wear out in the books.
stmt.bs.equipment.why: Machines you bought, at what you paid less wear.
stmt.bs.businesses.why: Each business at its equity: what it owns less what it owes, never below nothing.
stmt.bs.loans.why: What you still owe the lenders, not counting interest.
stmt.bs.interest.why: Interest counted since the last payment and not yet paid.
stmt.bs.worth.why: What you own less what you owe.
stmt.why.firstYear: This is your first {season}: nothing last year to set it beside.
stmt.why.account: Everything the books counted under this heading across the season.
stmt.why.dropped: The day-by-day list is kept for the last 8 seasons; this one is older.
stmt.why.cashRow: Every movement behind this row is listed above: day, what, whom, amount.

lenders.subtitle: Choose a lender
hub.why.trendChange: Over these seasons: {coins} in today's coins; {counted} as counted then; prices rose {prices}.
hub.why.trendText: Net worth counted at each close, restated in today's coins by the price index of that close, so a rise is a real rise, not only prices.
hub.why.made: What your wealth is made of
hub.why.madeText: Each share is of everything you own, before what you owe. A pie that is mostly land is wealth you can't spend; cash is what pays the bills.
hub.why.debtOwe: What you owe: loans and interest due
hub.why.debtText: What you owe divided by what you own, rounded down. Under {comfortable} is comfortable, over {risky} is risky: one bad season could cost you land.
hub.why.emergencyText: Cash and savings divided by what the next season close takes, rounded down. Your family's living counts at the basic plan at least. Under one season is amber.
hub.why.passiveRent: Rent from your houses and godown
hub.why.passiveBusiness: Profit of businesses run by a hired worker
hub.why.passiveText: Last season's income that came without your own labour, against your family's living. A business that lost money counts against it. The farm isn't counted: you still decide and sow.
savings.title: Savings deposit
savings.subtitle: At the co-op bank. Yours to take out any time.
savings.interestNext: {amount} at the next close, added to the deposit
savings.interestNone: Put something in and it earns at every close
savings.pricesNote: Cash in hand earns nothing and loses value as prices rise. A deposit earns, so it roughly keeps up.
savings.putNone: Not enough cash to put in
savings.standing: If cash runs short at the close
savings.standing.ask.note: Nothing leaves your savings unless you say yes the day before.
savings.standing.always.note: For a close you'll be away for: the bank pays what's short from your savings, and your season report says so.
savings.standingNote: Interest is Other money, not farm profit. The bank never lends against your deposit, and no lender can take it.
alert.closeShort: Short at the close by {short}: {who}. It takes {total}; you have {cash}.
alert.closeShortCovered: Your savings will cover {amount} at the close. You said yes.
season.savingsCould: Could cover {amount}. Nothing is taken unless you say yes.
season.savingsYes: You said yes: {amount} comes from your savings at the close.
season.savingsAlways: Your standing choice: {amount} comes from your savings at the close.
notify.CloseShort.title: The season's close is short of cash
notify.CloseShort.body: Open the game before it ends: your savings, the store or a loan can cover it.
why.away.Savings: The co-op bank added the season's interest to your deposit, and where it says your savings paid the close, a yes from you (or your standing choice) covered what your cash couldn't.
ledger.savingsCover: Your savings paid the close, with your yes
hub.why.savingsText: Put in and take out any time. The interest is added to the deposit at every close, before the statements, so it earns interest too. It counts in your emergency fund and in passive income, never as collateral, and no lender can take it.
hub.why.pricesDeposit: What the deposit earns a season
hub.why.pricesText: Prices rise a little every season. Cash in hand loses that much value. A deposit earns more than prices usually rise, so the savings keep up.
hub.why.standing: If cash runs short at the close
hub.why.standingText: Ask me: on the last day of the season you're warned, and nothing leaves your savings unless you say yes. Always pay from my savings: the bank pays what's short from your savings at the close, up to what you hold, and the season report says so.

milestone.title: Milestones · {n} of {of}
milestone.note: Just a way to see how far you've come. Nothing is given for a milestone.
milestone.firstLakh.done: Your cash and savings, less what you owe, reached a lakh.
milestone.firstLakh.todo: Cash and savings, less what you owe: {have} of {target}.
milestone.firstLakh.why: Your cash plus your savings deposit, less every loan and its interest, counted at a season's close. Borrowed cash is cash, but you owe it, so it doesn't count. The target is {target}: a lakh, whatever prices do.
milestone.twiceInherited.done: Your net worth reached twice the estate you started with, in today's coins.
milestone.twiceInherited.todo: Net worth {have} of {target}: {times} times your {inherited} inheritance, in today's coins.
milestone.twiceInherited.why: Your net worth at a close against {times} times what you inherited. The inheritance is counted in the coins of that close, so prices rising doesn't make it easier.
milestone.firstRent.done: A family paid you rent for the first time.
milestone.firstRent.todo: A family living on your land pays you rent.
milestone.firstRent.why: Reached at the first close where a family on your land had paid you rent.
milestone.debtFree.todo: Repay your last loan. A write-off at a foreclosure doesn't count.
milestone.debtFree.why: Reached when none of your own loans is open and the last one closed by being repaid. A foreclosure's write-off doesn't count, and a business's loan is on its own books.
milestone.passiveCoversLiving.done: Rent, interest and your hired businesses paid your family's living.
milestone.passiveCoversLiving.todo: Rent, interest and hired businesses cover {pct}% of your family's living.
milestone.passiveCoversLiving.why: Reached at a close where rent, interest on your savings and the profit of businesses you've hired out paid at least {pct}% of your family's living.
milestone.why.inherited: What you inherited, in today's coins
cash.row.4400.out: Interest on your savings, given back
alert.closeShortStill: Your savings will pay {saved} at the close, and you're still short by {short}.
season.moved.savedIn: Put into your savings, with its interest: still yours
season.moved.savedIn.why: Cash you put in the bank, and the interest the bank added to it. You still own it: it's in Your wealth, not a cost.
season.moved.savedOut.why: Savings back in your cash, or paid at the close when you said yes: not income.
season.InterestOnSavings.why: The co-op bank adds interest to your deposit at every close. It counts as money earned, but no cash comes: it stays in the deposit.
